Where it began

Stephen Fleming was born in Christchurch on 1 April 1973 and went to Cashmere High School, where he played rugby as well as cricket. Cricket won. He made his Test debut against India in March 1994 and announced himself with 92 and the man of the match award. Soon after, in his first one-day international, he made 90 not out. It was the start of a long habit of doing well when it counted.

The player

Fleming played 111 Tests from 1994 to 2008 and made 7,172 runs at 40.07, with nine hundreds and 46 fifties. His best was 274 not out, and in Cape Town in 2006 he became the first New Zealander to make three Test double-centuries. He held 171 catches, which ranks ninth among all Test cricketers, and few took more at slip.

He took charge of New Zealand at 23 years and 321 days, the youngest man ever to do so, and led them in 80 Tests, winning 28, more than any other New Zealand captain. Under him New Zealand won the ICC KnockOut Trophy in 2000, their first global title, took bronze at the 1998 Commonwealth Games and reached the 2007 World Cup semi-finals. He also led his country in 218 one-day internationals and in the very first Twenty20 international, against Australia in 2005.

What made him special

He was a graceful batter, at his best with the flick off the pads and the drives through cover and straight. But it was his captaincy that people remembered best. Shane Warne, who knew a thing or two about the game, rated him the best captain in the world.

The one thing he never quite mastered was turning fifties into hundreds: 46 of the first and nine of the second. Bowlers around the world probably thought that was quite enough.

Away from the middle

He led Nottinghamshire to the County Championship in 2005, their first for 18 years. Chennai Super Kings signed him as a player for the first IPL season and made him their coach in 2009, and over the years that followed they won five IPL titles and two Champions League titles under him. He also coached Melbourne Stars, Rising Pune Supergiants and the other Super Kings sides in South Africa and the United States, and in July 2026 he was named England's Test coach. In 2011 he was made an officer in the New Zealand Order of Merit, for what he had given to the game.

And finally

He was born on 1 April, but there was nothing foolish about the cricketer. If anything, the joke was on the opposition captains, who spent the best part of a decade trying to out-think him.
